In rising to address you, Mr. Speaker, in reply to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, I must say that I fail to quite understand the position he has taken on this question. That mav be due wholly to my fault or partly, perhaps, to his. True, he said he did not wish to discuss the economical aspects of the question, and therefore postponed any remarks he might have to make on the several items in the agreement before us. My hon. friend contented himself with a review of the past history of this country and its progress. He did not intend, he said, to go back and discuss the old Reciprocity Treaty of 1854, because that would be ancient history; but he did go back to 1866 and spent a large portion of his time in depicting the progress which Canada has made from that day to this. That progress was, of course, very gratifying to every member of this House; but my hon. friend failed to observe-perhaps it was by mistake-that the most notable progress which this country has made, has been made during the last 15 years during which, the Liberal party has administered its affairs. Any one who will look at the records of our trade cannot fail to be struck by that fact very forcibly. And no doubt the greatest factor in this progress, has been the carrying out by this government of a platforrn laid down 'by the Liberal convention in 1893.
Oh, oh.

I repeat that the change of element in that progress, has been the policy of this government, in carrying out that convention and making trade freer with the whole world, more particularly with Great Britain and the United States.
Hear, hear.

The Liberal party, in convention, assembled in this city in 1893, promised that should the people elect it to office, it would carry out the platform then laid down. Shortly after assuming office, steps were taken in the direction of making trade freer between Canada and Great Britain. The British preference was granted which gave a strong impetus to the trade of this country. At one bound our trade exceeded what it had ever reach-

ed before, under previous administrations. Our exports to Britain were, of course, admitted free into the English market, but we made trade between the two countries freer still, 'by reducing the duties on British goods, thus inducing a greater flow of British goods into this country and augmenting very materially the total trade between the two. We also made an honest effort to promote freer trade with our friends to the south. My hon. colleague and leader, the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), and another member of the cabinet early took action to see if anything could be done in that direction. In this they^ were not successful. The minds of our friends to the south were not then inclined to freer commercial intercourse, and from that day until a very short time ago, although we were ready at any time to listen to any proposal that might be for the benefit of both countries, we were unable to accomplish anything. However, to-day our friends to the south, are viewing things in a somewhat different light and are showing a disposition to have freer trade relations with us, and did make overtures to us to that effect. We met their approaches in the spirit in which they were made, with the result that my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), and myself have been able to effect an arrangement which we consider mutually advantageous, with reference to a large list of articles, under which these articles may enter each country absolutely free of duties, and with reference to ahother list of articles, on which the duties between the two countries have been made uniform. That arrangement was made, subject of course, to endorsation by this parliament. ^ My colleague, the Minister of Finance, is now affording this House an opportunity of pronouncing upon this arrangement, and that is the question we are at present discussing.
The agreement arrived at is a mutual one,_ subject entirely to the approval of parliament, both as to its acceptance today and as to its continuance. The fiscal independence of Canada remains to-day with this parliament and will continue to remain with it, under this arrangement precisely as it has done during past years. The same condition obtains with our friends in the United States. Their fiscal independence remains unaltered as well, but an understanding has been arrived at, which will take effect upon concurrent legislation being adopted by the people's representatives in both countries. Steps are_ now being taken in the Congress of the Lmted States to ratify that agreement, and that agreement is now before the Canadian parliament for its ratification.
We were told this afternoon that this thing should not be rushed. Well there 105$
is no disposition on the part of the government at all to rush the matter. This parliament will have all the time to consider it that it deems necessary. But it is necessary that we should consider it. It is in the interests of that country that we should do so, and I propose now to give my views of the benefit that will accrue to Canada from this arrangement, and likewise to the United States. But in doing so, I propose to refer to the objections, in the first place, which have appeared throughout the press of the country that is hostile to this understanding. One of these objections made in the press, but which has not been made by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, is that this House should not go into the matter at all until the people have been given an opportunity of pronouncing upon it. But how could you ever initiate any arrangement in such a manner as that ?
The arrangement was made in the only way in which it was possible to make it, and made on the responsibility of the ministry. They are responsible to parliament who are free to reject this arrangement if they choose to do so. The arrangement was made with the full knowledge on the part of the government, as there should be on the part of every member of this House, that the people themselves will have an opportunity of pronouncing upon it, and that at a not very distant date; and! I venture to say that when an election is held this will be a live question with the people of Canada, that they will pronounce-their judgment upon it-and I expect that that judgment will be favourable. If it Is not, and if the feeling should prevail that they want our friends on the opposition side who may be opposed to this to take the reins of government, these hon. gentlemen will have perfect freedom to submit a measure to this House to repeal this arrangement. I do not look for any such result as that.
We are said to be engaged in an entangling alliance. Nothing of the kind, there is no entanglement about it at all. 'it has been said that it will tend to do away with the British preference. There is nothing in these resolutions that points in that direction. The British preference remains-as my right hon. friend the leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) told the people of this country, whatever changes might be effected or negotiations entered into there is one cardinal principle that will be maintained, the British preference, and it is maintained. The argument is made that by what we have done we will weaken the tie that binds us to the empire as one of its members. What force, I will not say what sense, is there in that statement? The British preference remains, goods -will go to Great Britain as they have

gone before, goods will come from Great Britain as they have come before, and they will come with a preference over the goods that come from the United States in so far as there are duties upon these goods coming into this country under the general tariff. Therefore, I dismiss it at once, without offence I would say the statement is not worthy of intelligent men.
Under the present arrangement, typesetting machines come in from the United States free. How does the minister propose to give Great Britain a preference in that respect?

There are a great many things that come in free, agricultural products, for instance, all come in free. I do not know that we can do any more in the way of a preference for our British friends than to give them a bounty if they want to send us some of these things, but certainly if they come in free from the United States they will come in free from Great Britain too, and that is about as low as we can go for any country. Not only does it seem to me to be a remark not freighted heavily with common sense, but rather freighted with an imputation that is an insult in its nature, that is that because we have entered into an arrangement of this kind with our American friends, the tie of loyalty between this people and the British people will be in any way weakened. The loyalty of the Canadian people lies not in that direction, at least it does not on this side of the House.
Another objection that has been argued, and it was argued at length by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), this afternoon, is that this change of mind on the part of our American brethren is due in a large measure to their desire to reach and secure some of the natural resources of Canada. I do not know that I am concerned to deny that if anybody wishes to affirm it, but what did he specify as the natural resources of Canada? In one of the passages which he read, food products was said to be one of the most vital. If the people of the United States want to get some of our food products, that is not an unnatural thing on their part, nor do I think it is a very great disaster to the people of this country. If we have wheat and other grains more than we consume ourselves we will have to sell them to some one else, and the man who produces them, I think, will not be very careful or anxious as to the nationality of the man who buys them, he will be more concerned about the man who will give him the highest price. But they say:	You
should conserve your natural resources, and keep them for the people of this country. All right, do not let us ship away any more of these breadstuffs, do not let us sell ourselves out so we will be in danger Mr. PATERSON.
of want. But I can see no force in the argument that we should keep the whole of the crops of this Canada of ours stored up because, perchance, by and by, we will have great, great grandchildren enough to consume them all. They say the Americans want our natural resources that are buried in the hills, our ores. Well they do, I believe, in a measure, but we want to sell these ores. Do the men of Frontenac and Hastings want the iron ore that for centuries has lain in their hills undeveloped, giving no profit to the people of this country, to remain there because perhaps sometime in the future our great, great grandchildren may establish a smelting furnace? If they do there will be enough of those ores left there to establish all the furnaces they want. Meanwhile are you to keep them locked up there? The men of Frontenac will not tell you so. The Kingston Board of Trade asked my colleague and myself, instead of placing impediments in the way of the export of these ores, to endeavour to have the Americans take the duty off them, and we tried our best to get them to do it. They met us partially, but they could not, in their own interests as they saw it, place these ores absolutely on the free list. But iron ore is reduced from 15 cents as it was, to 10 cents. From conversation I have had with parties interested. I believe that as a result there will be a fine industry created in the county of Frontenac, giving employment to hundreds of men, and yet hon. members opposite say:	Lock it up, lock it up, do not
have these men employed.
Representations were made to us by the proprietors of talc mines in the county of Hastings. They said there was a duty of 25 per cent upon that article. They said to us:	There is a duty of 35 per cent
on that article, we have immense stores of it, there is no market for it here, there will be no market for it here for years and years to come. By a ruling they made it more than 25 per cent, they made it equal to from 50 to 60 per cent, and they have shut us out of their market. And that would suit my hon. friends opposite, the Americans shutting themselves out from getting this article. But it did not answer our purpose, at least we thought not, and what is the result? We prevailed upon the United States, not only to reduce it to the old rate of 20 or 25 per cent to which it had been raised by a ruling of a treasury board, but we got them to put it on the free list.
What was the article?
Talc.
Is that something used in place of soft soap?

No, it is not used for that, I think that in its finer preparation

it is not used in particularly large quantities. It goes finally, I think, into .the adornment of the person. Well, then, they say: You do not preserve our forests, you are going to allow them to be depleted. I have great sympathy with the preservation of our forests, I think reforestration and efforts in that direction are highly important. I am much pleased to know that a lively interest is being taken in that subject, and that steps will be taken towards reproducing the timber as it may be used. But let me point out to the leader of the opposition that these forests are not the possession of the Dominion government, they are the possession of the local legislature.
Not all of them.

I would like the hon. gentleman,to explain to the House that one clause about pulp. Is pulp going to be admitted into the United States generally, or is it going to be admitted only from such provinces as do not put an export or stumpage duty upon it? That question is now engaging the attention of the people of the United States, and they do not seem to understand it. The hon. gentleman has not explained the question to the House at all. He says it is free or it is not free.	,
I explained it as it is in the resolutions. The hon. gentleman can read them for himself.

There seems to be a difference of opinion in the United States, even in Congress, over the meaning of that clause. It is construed by some to mean that pulp and paper are to be admitted free forthwith; by others it is understood they will only be admitted from such provinces as do not put an export duty upon those articles in some form. Will the hon. gentleman explain that clause clearly to the House, and tell us what it means?
Well, I will leave the United States to settle their own matters.
I do not think that is right.
As far as we are concerned, that is the position we are in.
Evidently the hon. gentleman does not understand his own clause.
Oh, yes, the hon. gentleman understands it himself, but it may be impossible for me to make the hon. gentleman (Mr. Currie, Simcoe) understand it.
I confess I do not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The leader of the opposition was not once interrupted.

Oh, well, that does not bother me at all. I was saying that the point which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) laboured most, and where you could judge, perhaps, better from his utterances than from any other that he was opposed to this agreement, for I frankly confess that I was not quite sure, when he got through, whether he would vote for this
COMMON*!
proposition, or whether he would not, but the argument that he seemed to lay most stress upon was that we had spent millions and millions of money in developing our transportation system, and that it was largely in a line from west to east. He wanted to know why we should disturb this and expressed a fear that has been_ expressed in stronger terms than he did it in the newspapers opposed to this agreement, that our transcontinental roads would be interfered with, that the money that we had spent would have been, in a measure, wasted, that we were going to divert the traffic and have our grain carried through the United States, and that, therefore, it would be a very serious matter for us. Is the hon. gentleman aware that the United States roads south of Canada carry a large quantity of Canada's wheat to Great Britain and Europe now, with a duty on?
Carried in bond.

Carried in bond, without any cost as far as the bond is concerned. The hon. gentleman knows that. Well, if that be the case when the duty is on, as it is on now, and if that has been going on for years and years, w'hat harm has resulted from it in Canada? I read some remarks in a paper-I forget the gentleman's name, but I think he was the local member for Fort William, or Port Arthur, or something like that, and here is the wail that came from him. It was sad. He said: If you make wheat free it will go through American channels. Well, I had the curiosity to look up the figures in reference to that matter. He said: Our elevators that we have at Fort William and Port Arthur can be thrown into the bay if there is to be free wheat, because it will all go south. He seemed to be in blissful ignorance of the fact that out of that very Fort William elevator 12,292,771 bushels of grain went this year through the United States to England and Europe, and that out of the elevator at Port Arthur there went 7,186,142 bushels. This was wheat carried by our transcontinental railways, placed in the'elevators there, carried from thence through American channels to Great Britain and Europe. That has been going on for years, and yet you talk nonsense about diverting the traffic and ruining the railways when wheat can go as freely through American channels with 20 cents a bushel against it in the United States for home consumption, as it will go under this arrangement. These are samples of the arguments that we hear from hon. gentlemen opposite.
I wish to interrupt the hon. gentleman-
Order, order.

If he has the figures
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: An hon. member has the. right to ask a question and to interrupt with the permission of the hon. gentleman who has the floor, and until there is some intimation from the hon. gentleman who has the floor that he objects to the interruption I must allow the question to be asked.
Well, take it this time.
Will the hon. gentleman state what amount of western Canadian grain during the past year has passed through the Duluth and Superior elevators? He has the figures and he ought to know.

No, I have not got them. But I have my own figures here, which show that there was a total export of wheat through the United States of 25,950,728 bushels. Twenty-five million bushels lave gone in that direction, 19,000,000 or 20,000,000 of it right through Fort William and Port Arthur, and yet, because wheat is free-and it goes just as free to-day in bond-these elevators are to be taken down and thrown into the bay, if you would listen to the jeremiad of the local member, who spoke in that way. What will prevent wheat moving over our transcontinental roads in the future? If Mr. Hill, as they claim, should try to hold up and frighten the people, if he is going to project roads into the northwest here and there and extend those which he has there, do hon. gentlemen propose to prohibit him from bringing in those roads? Is that their policy? If he brings his roads in there or cieates new roads, if he carries western grain down over his roads and over to England, shipping it by American channels, he will have to do it as cheaply, if not cheaper, than our own roads, and if he does it cheaper, who gets the benefit but the men who grow the wheat? Sir, I say nothing against our great transportation Toads, but I do hope that they will not take up a position antagonistic to this arrangement, which is vital in the interest of the country out of any selfish motive.' We have aided these roads to the extent of millions and tens of millions. They have reached a sound financial position, and if they cannot get the grain at the present prices their self-interest will make* them lower their rates rather than give up the carrying of the grain. It was said-I am sorry to say- by a member of the British Columbia government that Mr. Hill was so anxious for this free wheat that he financed the deputation of farmers which came here. I am not disposed at all to deny that Mr. Hill may have ideas in his mind of reaching the

northwest by his present lines, or by more lines that he may propose. Mr. Hill is in the transportation business. The very papers that state that he finds himself cut off from his trade by other railways in the United States, and that he is casting longing eyes at our northwest in order to get our wheat. It would not be an unnatural thing for a railway man, a transportation man, to look for a source of supply, and Mr. Hill has no doubt come to the conclusion that I have come to, that you have come to, that every man has come to in this House, that there is going to be an enormous production of grain in our northwest, and if he does meditate coming in there to get a share of the carrying trade, and if he comes in there and gives rates to the people as good, if not better, than those that any other transportation road gives them, he will get that grain whether it goes through in bond or whether it be free, as it will be if this agreement passes.
Look at the report of the Department of the Interior and see the homestead entries for just one year, and then you may figure out what would be the effect upon transportation as regard railroads now in existence or which may hereafter be built. In the year 1910 there were 41,568 homestead entries made in the northwest, and of these, 13,566 were taken up by settlers from the United States representing 47 states and territories. From the older provinces of Canada there went 11,470 homesteaders and from the United Kingdom 7,331. These 41,568 homesteaders taken in one year comprise 6,650,880 acres, in addition to the 1,184,790 acres of land sold by the railway companies, the Hudson's Bay Company and other land owners. Just fancy that addition in one year to the land development of the west. The total area under crop, including wheat in 1909 was 11,960,000 acres and in wheat alone 6,778,000 acres and the total yield of wheat that year was 147,000,000 bushels and the average yield to the acre over 21 bushels. Have you figured out what this means ; have you considered, what facilities will be required to transport that enormous quantity of grain from the wheat fields in the west. Put it at only 100,000,000 bushels and to transport it would require 17 trains daily for 300 days, each train having 20 cars with 1,000 bushels of wheat in each car. And, Sir, it is counted upon as a certainty by those who know that within the next five years that production of wheat will be doubled and there will be all the wheat that James J. Hill, the Canadian Pacific railway, the Canadian Northern, and the Grand Trunk Pacific will be able to haul. Mr. Hill, may look forward better than some of you gentlemen opposite ; Mr. Hill may be more farseeing than most of you. To-night we have had the keynote of the Conservative attitude on this question, and
it is : Don't rush, go slow, we are well enough now, let things alone.
Hear, hear.

Hear, hear said my hon. friend but my motto is : When you are doing well let things alone unless you can do better. And we can do better. And, men like J. J. Hill can see in the future what hon. gentlemen opposite are blind to, namely, that there will be as great a change in this country and perhaps as great advancement in the next five years as there has been in the past ten. And so we will go on advancing and advancing, and yet, we have the leader of the opposition rising to frighten the people of this country from a trade agreement that will redound to tha wealth and prosperity of our people, because perchance, as he says, it may interfere with the business of our freight transportation lines. Well, Sir, cheaper rates there may be for the man who grows the grain, and he will not be found grumbling very much at that, but more grain there wili be for the railways to haul. I think I can say without egotism that I know a little about trade, and in my judgment the agreement now before you for ratification, if carried into effect, will give a stimulus to the prosperity of this country equal to if not greater than that which ' followed our inauguration of the British preference, against the protest of hon. gentlemen opposite. I should have liked had we unanimity on this question : I should have liked to see hon. members rise above partisan feeling and consider with unbiassed minds what it means to get an open market for our agriculturists, our fishermen, our lumbermen, and our mining interests. Perhaps K may not give us a greater market for our manufactured goods, but will not our manufacturers be in as good a position as they are now, plus the fact that the population of the wheat fields being increased and prosperity being at)road in the land, they will have to produce more manufactured goods to supply the demand within our own border. I regret, Sir, that there is opposition to this proposal ; I regret it for the sake of hon. gentlemen opposite. I should have liked to see them rise to the occasion but if they fail to do so I can tell them this : That in spite .of their opposition, in spite of their cynicism and jeerings at measures which have been propounded by this government, they have had to admit that these measures were fruitful for the advancement of the happiness and prosperity of our country. Their whole argument is : Canada is more prosperous now than any country under the sun, and why meddle with things as they are, and, Sir, in arguing that way they are forced to confess that our measures for the promotion of immigration, the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, the

British preference, and all these policies which the Liberal party carries into effect in spite of the opposition of gentlemen opposite, have made Canada to-day a prosperous and progressive country. Well, I am sorry to say they appear unwilling to join us in this last patriotic movement for the benefit of the people of the country. All I can say, Mr. Chairman, is this, that the Liberal party, having taken these other steps that produced this prosperity, are strong enough and willing enough, if it is left to them alone to have the glory of it, to see that this, like the other measures, is carried to a successful issue.

Mr. Chairman, I hope that my hon. friend, who has dispensed so much wisdom in the short time that he has spoken, and has done it with such extreme clearness and distinctness of voice, will pardon me if I do not follow the points one by one, which he has been endeavouring to make. I am not tonight concerned at all in an endeavour to get the best of a man in argument. I am looking rather to getting at the rights of a question, which I think is important enough to engage the attention of Canada, and will be thought by the people of this country important enough to call for calm, sound and deep thinking and reasoning rather than declamation. In the course of my remarks I shall probably touch the points which my hon. friend has made to-night; but what impresses me at the present time, is the situation in which we find ourselves-a position which, in the first place, is unique. Neither in Canada, nor do I think in any other country, has such important fiscal legislation been undertaken in quite the manner in which this has been undertaken by the present government. In the next place, the situation, is one of extreme gravity. I may be wrong, but I have given a great deal of thought to trade matters in the course of my political life, and my conviction is that we have never had in Canada any question quite so important as this present one-any issue upon which hung more far-reaching consequences. The only one that, in my mind, approached it, was the struggle in 1891, when commercial union with the United States and discrimination against Great Britain was the slogan of hon. gentlemen opposite, and the cry around which centred one of the greatest political battles ever fought in Canada. I think it is a situation which involves in a large degree the fiscal freedom and poljtica] independence of Canada. In the fourth place, I think it is a question which is fraught with consequences greater than any of us can now see, but a sense of which comes to me and I believe to every thoughtful man in this country-fraught with grave consequences to the future of that' empire, Mr. PATERSON.
of which, up to the present time, Canada has been a shining and a noble part. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance appealed to history, going into a Tather long disquisition upon the record of reciprocity negotiations. Whether he did that by way of apology or as a defence for the proposal which he has made to us, I do not know. If it was the first, it was as good as any other old thing; if it was intended for the second, it is a defence, which I think, is inadequate, and which will not stand examination. History is very valuable, Mr. Chairman. It is valuable for what it teaches us to imitate; it is equally valuable for what it teaches us to avoid; and, if my reading of the history of reciprocity negotiations with the United States of America is correct, it is one which may well teach us what to avoid in the present and for the future. But, Sir, there is history and history, and you, Mr. Chairman, were no doubt quick to perceive that my hon. friend traced the history of reciprocity negotiations up to the year 1891, and then and there dropped it. Then occurred a long hiatus of twenty years in which he could appeal to no history with relation to negotiations for reciprocity with the United States of America. What did that mean, Sir? It meant that the old volume was then completed, sealed, and laid away, and that at that time a new volume was begun and a new record and a new history was initiated in this country. Am I right or wrong in that ? In 1891 the Liberal-Conservative party made its last endeavour for reciprocity with the United Staffs of America, and after the negotiations were ended and we returned home to Canada, the Liberal-Conservative,, party declared itself as done with reciprocity from the United States, of America, and that henceforth its duty was to develop Canada on the lines of its own self-dependence, and to look to the British market as the great, steady, stable market for our products. The old heresy had not yet been quite purged from the Liberal party, which pursued the quest until 1897. They went to Washington; they tried their efforts; they failed. They came back, and they made declaration in this House of Commons and elsewhere, that as far as they, as a party, were concerned, they were done with reciprocity negotiations with the United States of America. Let us invoke the record. In 1898, the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, according to ' Hansard,' spoke as follows in this House of Commons, respecting the negotiations and their failure to result in anything:
Canada to-day is not in favour of reciprocity. There was a time when Canadians, beginning with myself, would have given many things to obtain the American market, hut. thank Heaven, these days are passed and over.

That is strong language; and it expresses what I suppose it was meant to say. But after ten years more during which neither Liberal nor Conservative party raised the issue of reciprocity with the United States, my right hon. friend stood in the Imperial Conference in London, and before the assembled delegates of the empire made this statement:
There was a time when we were wanting reciprocity with the United States, but our efforts and our offers were put aside and negatived. We have said good bye to that trade and we now put all our hopes upon the British trade.
Could anything be more explicit as a repudiation, before the assembled delegates of the empire, of any desire for reciprocity, and a declaration that Canada had given up the quest and had put all her hopes in the British market? Later yet, in 1899, in this House of Commons, the same right hon. gentleman said:
Canada has opened her doors to Great Britain in the hope that she would ultimately receive similar preferential treatment from the mother country.
This is my warrant for saying that from 1891 the Liberal-Conservative party and from 1897 the Liberal party-that is both parties in this	country-had closed
the	door	on reciprocal negotiationswith	the	United States	and	hadopened up	a newer, broader	and	morepromising highway for our commerce. But there is corroborative evidence. In a general election, if there be any live issue, it comes out on the hustings. After 1897 had passed and the right hon. gentleman had	made	his repudiations,	we	went
through the elections of 1900, 1904 and 1908, and I challenge him to show that in any one of those three electoral contests, anywhere in this Dominion, he or any of his party advocated reciprocity with the United States as a policy. On the contrary, the ideas which he enunciated in the extracts I have read, were promulgated from platform to platform, and it is not too much to say that we came to the conclusion, and rightfully, that Canada, as a whole, endorsed the action of the two parties and took no stock in reciprocity. I need not elaborate that point any further.
__ It was significant that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance closed his history at 1891, since which time Canada has made great progress, signal progress, despite the burdensome load it has had to carry in the shape of a rather poor administration. We heard this afternoon wha.t was done, what was begun, and what is contemplated by this government. Again I want to ask mv right hon. friend, after this exposition of the situation, why this sudden change, and this renewed quest for reciprocity ? Is not that a pertinent question ?
Why the change ? You had buried reciprocity. You declared that you had buried it The country attended its obsequies and did not mourn nor weep; and after it had been buried for 11 years, by yourselves and for a longer time by the Liberal-Conservative party, what has brought it to life again ? Will some one answer that question. Where was the mandate of this government to take that question up, to go to these conferences, to make this agreement and to bring it to this parliament and demand that this parliament shall pass it as being the best policy for this country ? That you did not get a mandate from the people is plain enough. You had a mandate from the people to let it alone, if ever a mandate was given, after the repudiations of hon. gentlemen opposite and the acquiescence in those repudiations by the people of this country at large. There were no compelling condition to force you on this question. Production was good. Never in the history of Canada has its production, in all its varied interests, been larger or richer. No blight had fallen on the productive powers of Canada, in any respect, owing to conditions which the government might remove. There was no lack of market for everything that Canada produced. There was quick sale, easy sale, no glut ip the markets, no molding in our bins and cellars, no rotting in our fields. Everything that Canada produced, and she produced richly, found a market and a ready market. There was no lack of .transport, everything ready for market had means of transport. The prices too were good, they were never better in Canada. I have just gone through a very important and useful volume which has been issued by the government itself, giving the round of prices for a series of years in this country, and the government themselves being the authority prices in the Dominion of Canada were never so high as they have been during this last five or six years. Where then were the compelling conditions in this country which cried for relief and for which relief could be got only by going to Washington and negotiating for a reciprocity treaty ? There were some few causes of dissatisfaction; we may reduce them to three. There was the demand of the grain growers in the w'est for free agricultural implements, or a reduced duty upon them. There was the fitful cry of the ardent and conscientious free trader, who with all the nower that was in him, cried for free trade, but supported the protectionist government of my right hon. friend, which rose here and there throughout the length and breadth of the country, and there was, in the third place, the wide spread dissatisfaction with the condition of things imposed upon us by the
COMMON d
United States of America in accepting a $104,000,000 free list from us and giving us but a $33,000,000 one in return, in buying from us but $100,000,000 worth, while selling to us $223,000,000 worth; of meeting a Canadian tariff of 26 per cent by a United States tariff of 411 per cent. There was a feeling in the country that that was not a neighbourly thing for them to do, not fair business treatment, not what we would expect from a great and rich and powerful neighbour. These were the three things that were mooted as grievances in the country.
I appeal to you, Mr. Chairman, as a man of common sense, if the grain growers and farmers in Canada believed that agricultural- implements were rated too high and that the government should either reduce the rate or make them free, I ask you, Sir, as a man of common sense what was- the scientific, the common sense, the business thing to do? It was for them to lay their plaint before their own, government and if they made good their case to get the grievance removed by tariff legislation in this House of parliament. That was the straightforward, the common sense, the business method of procedure. If their case was good, the government should have granted them relief; if their case was not good, the government, with equal strength and justice should have said to them: You are treated as well as others and we think you have no cause for complaint. The second one could have been met, was in process of being met, had this government simply remained at home and minded what the people had told them to do and avoided what the people had not given them any mandate for doing. In the United States of America what was the condition of things? A high tariff from time immemorial, growing higher through the Dingley Bill, the McKinley Bill and at last coming to a height of 42 per cent on an average on dutiable goods; against that a revolt broke out, a campaign was waged, and the slogan of the campaign in the Republican party was a downward revision of the tariff of the United States. The Republican party promised it; they were elected, they came into power, they brought dowm their measure and the Payne-Aldrich Bill ended not in any revision downward that was worth mentioning, but, in some things in a revision upwmrds. What happened? The people of the United States have a pretty sterling sense of wdiat is due from them to men who make pledges and then break them and they rose in insurrection. When the Payne-Aldrich Bill was going through Congress some Republicans raised the banner of insurrection in the Congress and in the Senate. They fought the Bill there, thev were defeated there, they carried the fight out into the constitu-Mr. FOSTER.
encies and in the late elections they gained the support of the people and the punishment which ought always to come upon men who make pledges and then cynically break them came to the Republican party. They w^ere defeated in the country and their day is just about over in the Congress of the United States and will soon be over in the Senate of the United States. What was the position? That insurgent force that swept the Republicans out of power was pledged to a diminution of the tariff especially on food stuffs. The Republican party in that position, the Democratic party were pledged to a revision downward of the tariff especially on food stuffs. It was known by all _ men that the new Congress soon -to go into power would deal with that matter and it was known that it would deal with it in the line of taking off and diminishing duties especially upon natural resources and food stuffs. That was the moment when this government should have avoided any meddling in tariff negotiations with the United States of America, but that was the psychological moment, as my hon. friend said, when he took it into his head to butt in and pay the Republican party for what was due and acknowledged to be due to the people of the United States, and what that narty would have to give at the coming session of Congress. That is the way that matter would have been settled and settled with better effect than by the present arrangement and without our having to foot the bills in any way.
That being the case wdiat happened? Just at that psychological moment-I think that is a good word-two men started out of Ottawa, two very estimable men, but not in any way extraordinary. Apart from their being ministers of a government, members of a cabinet, just lay aside their titles, and their positions, and their pov'er of dispensing patronage, and turn them out in the streets of Montreal or Toronto, and you would not find all the captains of industry, and the men of finance, and the great -business men of the country, rushing out and falling down before them, sitting at their feet, and worshipping them ; not at all. They are estimable men. But -does the Minister of Customs mean to tell us to-night in sober earnest that he knows more about the business of this country than the trained business men who have been in it, in one branch or another, from boyhood up, and are to-day the great captains of industry and men famous in their several spheres? Not at all. Neither would my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, though a very good newspaper man in his time, -and though a very good man in business in a limited way-I do not know that he has had any specially large experience, himself sav here in the House to-night that he knows more about these things than the
33X3

trained men of business who direct affairs in this Dominion of Canada. Now, Sir, what happened? These two estimable men, without any mandate from the people, without any call from any interest in this country-that is literally true-without any consultation with any interest from British Columbia to Cape Breton, these two men journeyed to Washington, consulting with nobody, except thirteen not more extraordinary men, with whom it is just possible they consulted, though I do not know-men of such eminence in business affairs as the hon. the Minister of Labour (Mr. King), men so versed in financial and high matters of banking and commerce as the hon. the Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden), men so famous in business circles as the hon. the Secretary of State (Mr Murphy), men of such fine financial mind and business acumen as the right hon. gentleman himself who leads the government and the party (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). Now, giving all credit to those men for all that they know-and they know a lot, a lot that they ought never to have known-but gi\ ing them credit for all they know, it was true that in the whole Dominion of Canada no one was consulted but these fifteen men, if even they were all consulted. What did the right hon. gentleman say himself? He passed through the west this year, he was asked for tariff reductions and tariff adjustments. What did he promise to the deputations? That lie would take it into consideration, but there would be no adjustment of the tariff until a tariff comission had examined into the matter, and had heard from the various interests. Did my ngfit hon. friend make that promise in the west? If he did not, will he deny it now? The right hon. gentleman did make that promise, he will not deny it now. Has he carried out his promise?
There is another thing the right hon. gentleman said: To one cardinal principle we adhere, that is that the British preference would not be interfered with. Did the right hon. gentleman make that promise? Did he mean it when he made it? Has he implemented that promise any more than the other? A solemn promise made by a leader.of a government to men who came to him with a tariff grievance that he would not make any adjustment of the tariff until -common sense idea-a tariff commission had been issued, and had found out the facts of the case, and got information upon which to make an adjustment. And yet he has made the most important tariff revision that ever was made in this country, lr. the face of a promise that what-wer vas done the British preference would not be impaired, he comes back with an instrument which, in almost every line of it, impairs, diminishes or completely obliterates the preference which Great Britain has to-day in the markets of Canada.
These two men sit down with three or four other men in a secret chamber in Washington. The receiver is taken off the hook, the telegraph line is cut, and for two weeks those gentlemen are closeted in camera with gentlemen of the United States, and no interest in this Dominion can get a word to them or a word from them. There are rumours, there are grave stories of what is being done, there are fears everywhere, and dislocation and disturbance in, every part of this country. The receiver is still off the hook, the line does not run into the room. No interest in Canada can get the ear of that conclave of four or five men who are dealing with the affairs of this nation. How do they deal with.them? On the line of justice and fair play? No, Sir. It is a strong word, but I ,am going to use it, they dealt with these interests as gamblers, deal. Now that I have used it, I will show you that I am not iar out of the way. If an interest comet to a government which is independent., which rules in Canada, responsible only to parliament, and that interest says : We want more protection; or want less protection upon such and such a line of goods, there is only one way in which the grievance may be removed and justice may be done, that is, to look into each case. try it on its merits, giving to the one or taking from the other because of the intrinsic merits of that interest which has to be taken from or added to. Is there any man in this House, Grit or Tory, who can deny that this is the proper way to do it? Is that the way that these gentlemen in camera in Washington acted? Not at an, Sir. The United States player shoved up his pawn, free fish ; the Canadian player advanced his, free fruit. Before the Canadian player shoved up the pawn of free fruit, did he call before him the representatives. o.f that great and growing industry in this country, and by a .single word ask them what would be the effect of this change upon their great industry? He had to go one better, or one equal to the American player, but he did not do it on any ground of reason or of justice or examination. The American player put up free dairy products to tlie United States. The Canadian player shoved up his free dairy products to the Dominion of Canada. Did he say free dairy products because he had consulted the interests-the wide interests-of the dairymen of this country, and had advised that those interests would not be hurt, and might be advantaged by it? Not at all ; he was asked to play up in the game, he played and so it went from one interest to another until every pawn was moved and the game ended. All that time, the interests that you were playing with were in dense ignorance of what you were doing, and you were in

dense ignorance of how their interests would be affected by your play. That is absolutely the wrong way to deal with the interests of this or any other country in the matter of tariff legislation. Did I use too strong a word? I do not think so. I was not vicious in using the word ; I just meant it, that is all.
And now, Sir, after having played the game they take the receiver off the hook, they connect the telephone with the chamber, and they let this parliament know that they have signed a pact. What kind of a pact? Did you, in Winnipeg, know what it was? Did you in Wentworth, did you in Brantford, did you in Kent, did any of you members of parliament who represent mightly big interests many of you, large interests all of you, know one single thing of what had been done behind your back and behind the back of this country? No, Sir, you did not. Now, Sir, the crime -for it is not much less than that-might have been mitigated if one course had been taken. Having no mandate, having consulted nobody, taking it up off your own bat-the crime would have been mitigated or I could not have called it such if you had brought that pact back to Canada and stood up in parliament and said: This is what we have done; true, we had no mandate; true, we held no consultations, but this is what we have done, and, having done what we thought best for Canada, we present that pact to the electorate of this Dominion and invite them to consider it and to pass their opinion upon it. If they had done that they would have followed the constitutional practice, they would have honoured responsible government, they would have been true to the democracy about which they talk so much, they would have approved themselves as business men and as statesmen, who have confidence in the people and do things above board. But that pact is signed, is brought back to parliament when we are half through this session and parliament is told that it must be passed without the dotting of an ' i ' or the crossing of a ' t.' Take the whole of it or take none of it! The Minister of Finance has the colossal boldness to stand up in this parliament and fling before it that pact gotten up by two men without mandate, consultation, or authority from anybody, or any great interest, and then cooly says that parliament is absolutely free to take it or not, as parliament pleases. No wonder sotne of my friends opposite smile. The Minister of Finance knows that he was stating what theoretically may be true, but is practically absolutely false. This parliament is free! I invite my right hon. friend now to carry out the words, implemented the statement of the Minister of Finance and to-morroiw take the free voice of your party in this parliament, let every Mr. FOSTER.
man vote as he chooses and pleases, and so prove say that this parliament is free. Will he do it? Will he do it? Not for his life will he do it. This parliament is free, but the government has pledged itself as a government to use its utmp.st efforts to pass that measure through parliament. If the government does not pass it through the government dies. If the government dies the party dies, and. therefore, the party is bound to support the government if it fears and flies from death and dissolution. Death is repulsive in every form, none the less so in its political forms, and the amount of freedom we have in this parliament and in this country is measured by the fact that the government has pledged its existence to the passage of this measure, and that if it fails not the government alone, but the party in the House and in the country in all its ramifications goes out of power and another party comes in. When I was listening to the Finance Minister going so glibly over his story, and as the extent and gravity of the measure forced itself to my mind I wondered whether the Finance Minister himself knew in any adequate degree or measured the full import of the agreement. Giving him all credit for far-seeing capability just as freely as I can give it to him, I have no hesitation in saying that he did not then know, he does not know now and I have not yet found a man in Canada who does know just where all this may end.

If the people ever perish it will be because of their lack of knowledge, and I have not the least doubt that if the situation in its entirety can be put before the people of this country my right hon. friend will find that he is in the great minority. My right hon. friend, in that contingency would have to sit down and with emphasis. Now, what does this measure do? In the first place it alters the fiscal conditions of interchange, not for a few unimportant articles, but a long list of most important products. It alters the fiscal conditions of interchange for all our dairy products, all our animals, all our grains, a large nronortion of our lumber, all our natural food products, all our fish products except sardines, all our fresh vegetable products, our mineral products, our wood pulp and paper, by transferring them in one block from the dutiable to the free list. Do we know just what that means and can we sense just exactly how far that reaches? But it goes further than that:	Our meat products, our grain pro-

ducts, our prepared vegetables and food products, a large slice of manufactures, are transferred to a lower reciprocal list, and another fairly large number of important products are transferred to a non-reciprocal but specified list in which the duties are lower. In gross, it takes $95,000,000 of products and at a stroke of the pen transfers them from dutiable to free or from a higher dutiable to a lower dutiable list. Every man knows that if you change the fiscal conditions of interchange of $95,000,000 worth of products in this country you affect in some degree every other of our products or nearly so. As I have shown $47,800,000 of our imports, and $47,300,000 of our exports are affected. Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not want to labour these different points beyond what is necessary to get them under advisement and thought. Every man in this House must realize the importance of a measure which at one stroke of the pen lifts $95,000,000 of interchangeable products out from old established conditions and makes a different fiscal system for interchanging them. Such a measure must be of a far reaching and wide importance. How far it goes requires business men of the best calibre to figure out adequatelv. But, this arrangement does something even more important: It shifts the base and conditions of production. It is true that production is of greater importance than interchange or trade, because trade is founded upon production and without products you cannot have trade. You must have at least two different productions in order to have a trade; one man raises one thing, another man raises another thing and there you have the basis of interchange and that interchange you nfeasure by your trade figures of the value of each. Therefore, though trade is important, the conditions and the base of production is more important still 'to be considered. And, this agreement if it goes into operation, shifts the base of production and not to the advantage of Canada in my opinion. For example, British Columbia is particularly adapted to the raising of fruits, and British Columbians have invested their capital and risked their future in the business and they have done well and aim to do better. They have accomplished their success so far through being fairly protected from the southern fruit growers who compete in their market. There you have the production of fruit that employs labour and capital and is of great importance to that province. East of the Rockies they produce grain and cattle; British Columbia has to get grain and the prairies have to get fruit, and there you have the basis of interchange between these two parts of our Dominion, and the products are both raised in Canada. Now, what does this measure do? It changes the base of
production; it says to the prairie buyers: Men in the United States will raise fruits and will supply them to you and you need not deal any more with British Columbia: it says to the prairie provinces: You may still raise grain and cattle, but you will send them down to the United States. You have the same grain and cattle raised, you have the same fruit raised, but one of your products has been shifted from its base in Canada and transferred to the United States. That, Sir, is the defect of this instrument which is before us to-night. These gentlemen opposite say: We are in favour of reciprocity? Are you? What would be the best reciprocity?-Reciprocity between the 'different sections in Canada itself that raise different productions and have different capabilities. Why, if you favour reciprocity. should you kill, or deteriorate, or diminish the reciprocity between British Columbia and the prairies? That is but a sample, but there are other instances. Take fish which is a great natural industry and a great business industry as well. Within the last 20 years a fish trade of large dimensions has been built up between the lower provinces and the rest of Canada running as far as the Rockies.
There is a production in Canada. The eastern Canadians want cattle, want grain, or want flour, which is raised in the western provinces. There are the elements of a reciprocity which builds up this country- both productions made in Canada and an interchange between the different sections of Canada. Now, what are. you going to do? You are going to say to the fish industry in the eastern provinces: Go, seek your markets somewhere else. The fishermen of the lakes and the fishermen of the Atlantic shore, because they have shorter routes and cheaper routes, maybe, to the heart of the great west, will get and give the fish that are required in the west. It will no longer be reciprocity between two sections of our own country. It will be reciprocity between the United States in one production and the west in another production. Now, Sir, that runs through the whole of this reciprocity arrangement. You talk about your foreign trade, and you bellow about it as though it were the greatest thing in Canada. I was going to say that it was almost the least thing in Canada. What is the greatest thing in Canada? The interprovincial trade, which is' founded upon the many productions in the east, and the wheat, grain and cattle productions in the west- the two complementing each other. What has made Canada so strong, and so great in her progress is this, that you have filled her veins with the rich blood of interprovincial trade, stimulating productions, in various parts, and then interchanging these productions one part with the other part.

I do not feel like finishing my speech to-night, and with the consent of the House, I would move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.
